slides.title: Keys
slides.say:
SAY: This branch of the chapter starts from a payment. Alice wants to pay Bob, but the thousands of full nodes that will verify her transaction do not know who Alice or Bob are, and the design is meant to keep it that way, to protect their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.concept: A number, a curve, and a one-way multiplication

slides.title: The 1976 paper that split the key in two
slides.say:
STORY (1976-11): In November 1976 two Stanford researchers published 'New Directions in Cryptography', opening with a sentence that aged well: 'We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.' Their idea - a key split into a public half and a private half, tied by a one-way computation - is the exact machinery this chapter runs: multiply a point, publish the result, keep the multiplier. Forty years later the ACM gave them the Turing Award for it.
SOURCE: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), November 1976; ACM A.M. Turing Award 2015. Photo: Wikimedia Commons 'Diffie and Hellman', CC BY-SA 3.0.
slides.concept: Public and private halves - one 1976 idea under every address

slides.title: A private key is just a number
slides.say:
SAY: A private key is simply a number, picked at random. Control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key: the key is used to create the signatures that spend bitcoins by proving control of the funds used in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why is a password a bad private key even if it is long?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - PrivateKey, Entropy.
slides.concept: Any 256-bit number - the hard part is choosing it unpredictably

slides.title: The curve everyone agreed on
slides.say:
SAY: The name secp256k1 identifies the specific elliptic curve and the set of constants that Bitcoin uses. The curve is y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p, with p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Who chose these constants - and why does 'nothing up my sleeve' matter?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Secp256k1, GeneratorPoint.
slides.concept: secp256k1: two primes, one base point, shared by all

slides.title: Double-and-add: the one-way street
slides.say:
SAY: Elliptic curve multiplication takes a point P and a whole number k and produces kP, which is defined as P + P + P + ... + P with k terms.
ASK: Where exactly does 'easy forward, hard backward' live in these 13 lines?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - PointMultiplication, DiscreteLogarithm.
slides.concept: 256 doublings forward - and no known road back

slides.title: Prove the key without showing it
slides.say:
SAY: A digital signature is a number that a signer computes from a message and from a private key. Anyone who has the message, the signature and the matching public key can verify the signature, that is, can check that it was produced by the holder of the private key and that the message has not been altered since.
ASK: What would 'showing the key' even mean here - and what breaks the moment you do?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - DigitalSignature, KeyControlProof.
slides.concept: Chapter 1's house key, kept honest: sign, never reveal

slides.title: Formats
slides.say:
SAY: This branch is about writing the same information down in different ways. A private key, a public key and a hash commitment are all numbers, and a number can be shown in binary, in hexadecimal, in a compact alphabet with a built-in checksum, or in a two-dimensional barcode.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Format.
slides.concept: The same numbers, dressed to travel

slides.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
slides.say:
STORY (2009-2010): Open src/base58.h in the source tree this course pins and the first thing after the copyright lines - 'Copyright (c) 2009-2010 Satoshi Nakamoto' - is a design memo. Why base-58 and not base-64? Because 0, O, I and l look alike in some fonts; because punctuation breaks selection and line-wrapping; because an all-alphanumeric string survives e-mail and double-clicks whole. Four human reasons, zero mathematics - the alphabet of every legacy address is a usability decision, documented by its author in the code itself.
SOURCE: src/base58.h at the corpus-pinned commit 05bc2f53 of bitcoin/bitcoin: the copyright line naming Satoshi Nakamoto (2009-2010) and the 'Why base-58 instead of standard base-64' comment, quoted verbatim on the slide (MIT).
slides.concept: The address alphabet is usability engineering, documented

slides.title: From key to WIF and back
slides.say:
SAY: The wallet import format, abbreviated WIF, is the text form in which a private key is exported from one wallet and imported into another. It is the base58check encoding of the version byte 0x80 followed by the 32-byte private key, and, for keys that produce compressed public keys, an extra byte 01 at the end (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Decode a WIF by eye: which characters can never appear?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - WalletImportFormat, CompressedPrivateKey.
slides.concept: WIF is the same number, dressed for transport

slides.title: The checksum that catches your typo
slides.say:
SAY: A checksum is a short value derived from a piece of data and attached to it. Anyone who has the data and the attached value can recompute the check and see whether they still agree; if the data was altered, they will with overwhelming probability disagree.
ASK: What does the checksum NOT protect you from? (the next story answers)
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Checksum, Base58Check.
slides.concept: Four bytes stop a mistyped address from costing coins

slides.title: Addresses
slides.say:
SAY: This branch turns the keys of the first branch into something one person can hand to another. An address is a short string that a receiver gives to a payer so that the payer's wallet can build a transaction output that only the receiver can spend.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - Address.
slides.concept: Commitments you can read out loud

slides.title: From public key to address, exactly
slides.say:
SAY: A pay to public key hash address, abbreviated P2PKH, is the legacy address in which the output script commits to the HASH160 of the receiver's public key. The output script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <commitment> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG and the spender's input script is the signature followed by the public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why hash the key at all - why not publish K as the address?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - P2pkhAddress, Hash160.
slides.concept: Two hashes and an alphabet - the pipeline, executed

slides.title: The address that eats coins
slides.say:
STORY (since 2011; balance fetched 2026-10-06): Spell a message inside an address, append a valid checksum, and you get 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE - a perfectly valid address whose matching key nobody has, because it was chosen as text, not derived from a key. People send coins to it anyway: at this build it held 13.41747849 BTC across 5,832 deposits, and not one satoshi has ever left. The checksum protects you from mistyping an address; nothing protects coins sent to an address that commits to no key.
SOURCE: blockstream.info API, address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE, fetched 2026-10-06 during this build: funded 1,341,747,849 sat over 5,832 outputs, spent 0 - the figures pinned in EATER below.
slides.concept: An address commits to a key - it cannot conjure one

slides.title: SegWit and bech32: the second alphabet
slides.say:
SAY: Segregated witness, shortened to segwit, is an upgrade of the Bitcoin protocol that defines a new structure called the witness, committed to blocks separately from the tree of transactions. The structure contains the data required to check that a transaction is valid, but not the data that determines what the transaction does; in particular, scripts and signatures are moved into it (Lombrozo et al., 2015).
ASK: Read bc1q... aloud to a friend: which old-alphabet mistakes are now impossible?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - SegwitUpgrade, Bech32Address.
slides.concept: New addresses move the witness and drop the look-alikes

slides.title: Error detection, measured
slides.say:
SAY: Error detection is the property of a format that lets software notice that a string has been altered by an accident, such as a mistyped character.
ASK: Why does 'provably catches' beat 'has never missed so far'?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 4 - ErrorDetection, BchCode.
slides.concept: bech32m catches what base58 provably misses

slides.title: Taproot, and what wallets do today
slides.say:
SAY: Pay to taproot, abbreviated P2TR, is the output kind of segwit version 1. For a P2TR output the witness program is a point on the secp256k1 curve.
ASK: Which prefix will your first wallet hand you - and can you say why now?

slides.title: Habits the chapter prescribes
slides.say:
SAY: Address reuse is the practice of receiving more than one payment to the same address. Because all the transactions are public, every payment to an address is visible together with every other payment to it.
ASK: If one seed makes every address, what single thing must you back up?
